- Original land cost: Just over £5,500 in 1907.

- First match: Harlequins vs Richmond in October 1909.

- First international: England beat Wales 11–6 in January 1910.

- Rugby World Cup finals: 1991, 2015 and the 2025 Women's Rugby World Cup.

- First concert: The Rolling Stones in 2003.

- Wartime use: Horses and cattle grazed on the pitch during the First World War.

- Unofficial Springboks nickname: Twickersfontein.

title: Women's smaller ball trial extended into second season
article_text:
World Rugby has extended the women's 4.5 ball trial for a second season after releasing data showing improvements in several areas of the game and receiving "overwhelmingly positive" feedback from players and coaches.

Data collected from the Sevens trials showed ruck speeds were on average 10% faster, while a four-year trend of declining passing rates was reversed. Goal kicking accuracy was unaffected.

The 4.5 size ball will be used in the 2026-27 HSBC SVNS Series and Championship, starting on 28 November in Dubai.

World Rugby confirmed that a decision on the 4.5 ball for the whole of the women's game would be taken in February, with data from the XVs game still being gathered.

The smaller ball debate has split opinion, with many England players expressing their dislike of the trial, including fly-half Zoe Harrison describing it as the "worst decision ever" earlier this year.

However, Wales wing Lisa Neumann is a fan, saying "it's changed the game" for her passing because of improved grip on the ball.

The data gathered in Sevens compares four seasons of size 5 ball data with one season using the 4.5 ball.

The home nations played with the 4.5 ball in the recent WXV tournament but those who have returned to Premiership Women's Rugby (PWR) are back playing with a size 5.

World Rugby confirmed that PWR declined the opportunity to use the smaller ball this season, while New Zealand's Super Rugby Aupiki and Australia's Super W opted to use the 4.5.

World Rugby's Chief Player Welfare and Rugby Sevens Officer Mark Harrington confirmed that the timing of the trial is specific.

"This was the window of the 12 to 18 month period where it didn't necessarily conflict with Olympic qualification or Rugby World Cup qualification," he said.

"Wherever we land [in February], it's the same ball for both codes."

Should World Rugby decide to adopt the 4.5 ball, Head of Women's Game Sally Horrox said: "There'll need to be some proper planning and a sensible transition.

"You don't want to put that burden on the game or that opportunity on the game without having the chance to plan."

She also confirmed that support for the community game would be taken into consideration if changes were implemented.

"We are considering the economics of the situation and any phase change or rollout," she added.

"If a change is recommended, then we, the unions and the high-performance committee would weigh up the costs, the supply and the impact on the community game before anything happened. That would be part of the conversation in February."

Additional reporting by Alex Brotherton.

title: Matt Fagerson out of Scotland showdown as Nathan McBeth handed injury boost
article_text:
Matt Fagerson has returned to Glasgow Warriors after suffering a jaw injury in Scotland’s 67-5 Nations Championship victory over Japan at Murrayfield. The back-row forward will miss Sunday’s seventh-place showdown with Argentina at Twickenham.

Duhan van der Merwe has also left the Scotland camp and returned to Edinburgh Rugby. The winger has not featured in any of Scotland’s three Tests this month and will now focus on his club return.

There is more encouraging news on Nathan McBeth, who remains with the squad. The Glasgow Warriors prop was forced off with an ankle injury against Japan, but the problem is not considered as serious as first feared.

Scotland head to Twickenham having beaten Australia and Japan in their last two outings, while Argentina arrive following a 45-17 defeat by France.

Recent history should offer further encouragement. Scotland beat the Pumas 47-38 in Córdoba in July and have won seven of the countries’ last 11 meetings.

Argentina, though, memorably fought back from 21-0 down to win 33-24 at Murrayfield last November.

title: All Blacks: New Zealand Rugby boss gives blunt verdict on Dave Rennie’s coaching future
article_text:
All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie has the “full support” of New Zealand Rugby (NZR), according to the governing body’s chief executive Steve Lancaster.

Rennie took over the All Blacks’ coaching reins from Scott Robertson earlier this year but the men in black have had mixed results in the international arena as they have already lost five out of 12 Tests played so far in 2026.

Under Robertson’s guidance, New Zealand won 20 out of 27 Tests played over a two-year period from 2024 to 2025 and they suffered four defeats during last year’s international campaign.

The All Blacks went down to a 3-1 defeat against their arch-rivals the Springboks during the four-Test Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series, before Wales claimed a shock 35-28 victory New Zealand in Cardiff recently and they then fell to a record 37-12 loss against England this past weekend.

Lancaster said despite all those defeats, NZR still believe that Rennie is the right man to lead the All Blacks.

“I’ve told Dave that and I’m happy to, you know, state that publicly that, you know, we, Dave has our full support,” Lancaster told Radio New Zealand. “We’re confident that we have the right person coaching this team, no question in our minds.”

Lancaster also revealed that the All Blacks players are backing Rennie to continue leading the team. “I’ve had the benefit of being in this team environment over the course of this year and they’re a very strong and aligned group,” he said.

“There’s clear leadership. The team are behind Dave, but they know what they have to achieve. The last two weeks’ performance is really disappointing and we need to understand how that’s come to pass, but no question over Dave being the right person to lead the team.”

Although the All Blacks’ record in 2026 is not of a high standard, Lancaster is adamant that there has been growth and meaningful improvements under Rennie’s leadership during the season.

“In terms of what we’re seeing within the team environment, within the way the team is performing, notwithstanding the last two weeks, which we’re absolutely going to have to own and understand, we’ve seen some positive shifts,” he explained.

The All Blacks looked weary in their defeat against England as they came off second best in most departments. Many rugby enthusiasts have questioned whether the men in black’s physically draining series against the Springboks is taking its toll on them at this late stage of the season.

Lancaster feels it’s worth investigating whether fatigue contributed to New Zealand’s recent defeats against Wales and England.

“We probably, neither ourselves nor South Africa, fully appreciated just how gruelling that Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series was,” he said.

“Those four Tests were unbelievable in their intensity, the quality of the rugby, but South Africa have lost their last two matches, three of their last four and we’ve lost our last two.

“We will have to look deeper to understand whether that has been a factor or not and if it has, what we need to change to ensure that we don’t see that again.”

The All Blacks suffered a major setback at the start of their current tour of the United Kingdom when the team’s head of security, Logan Cadwallader, passed away in Edinburgh a few days before their Test against Scotland which they won.

Lancaster believes Cadwallader’s death has also affected the side but he said the All Blacks are determined to bounce back when they face England in a rematch in Nations Championship’s third-place playoff at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham on Saturday.

“There’s no lack of resolve or motivation,” he added. “There wasn’t going into last week either, right? So that’s kind of what makes it a little bit inexplicable, but the team will absolutely be doing everything they can to get up and finish the year on a positive note.”

title: Scotland dealt Matt Fagerson injury blow ahead of final Nations Championship clash
article_text:
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Scotland will be without Matt Fagerson for their final Nations Championship clash.

The back-row forward suffered a jaw injury during Scotland’s 67-5 win over Japan on Saturday and has returned to Glasgow Warriors.

Duhan ven der Merwe has also been released back to Edinburgh ahead of Scotland’s final game against Argentina at Twickenham on Sunday.

The 31-year-old winger has not featured in any of Scotland’s three Murrayfield games this month.

The squad update did not mention Nathan McBeth, who was forced off with an ankle injury against Japan, although head coach Gregor Townsend previously stated the Glasgow prop was unlikely to make the game in London.

Nor was there mention of Rory Darge, who pulled out of the team with a shoulder injury before being replaced by Fagerson.

Darge had been due to captain Scotland in the absence of Sione Tuipulotu, who has a knee injury and was due to see a specialist.

The likes of Jack Dempsey, Ben White and Scott Cummings returned to their clubs last week because of injury.

title: Finals opener facing half-empty Twickenham and Springboks take Erasmus decision
article_text:
These are your headlines on the morning of Tuesday, November 24.

The Times report that South Africa decided against appealing the decision to suspend head coach Rassie Erasmus.

Erasmus put himself in hot water last week during a press conference following their defeat to France, claiming the officials made a number of on-field mistakes and suggesting there could be "match-fixing" at play.

World Rugby hit the double World Cup winner with a six-match ban in a lengthy statement, which you can read here.

South Africa released a statement of their own shortly afterwards, saying they were requesting a personal hearing for the 54-year-old.

The statement reads: “SA Rugby is requesting a full misconduct hearing for Springbok coach Rassie Erasmus following his sanctioning by an independent World Rugby panel for comments made in a press conference in Dublin on Monday.

“A SA Rugby spokesperson said that the organisation respected the process but had requested an opportunity for its coach to contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives.

“SA Rugby trusted that such a hearing could be expedited considering the seriousness of the charge, and will not make any further comment until the hearing could be completed.”

The Times' Will Kelleher now reports that SA Rugby never officially appealed the ban, so there will be be no formal hearing.

The Springboks take on France at Allianz Stadium Twickenham this weekend in the final of the Nations Championship, with Erasmus set to watch the game away from the stadium.

Sluggish ticket sales look set to blight the first night of the Nations Championship finals at Twickenham this weekend.

Friday’s double-header featuring Italy v Fiji and Ireland v Australia appears on course to be played out in front of a crowd of less than half the stadium’s 82,000 capacity.

The tournament’s official ticket website is showing swathes of tickets still available in most sections with the exception of the top tier, which is expected to be closed.

Officials acknowledged earlier this month that sales could be an issue, with fans having to wait until last weekend to discover the finalised schedule for the three-day showpiece.

Tickets for Saturday’s two games – Wales v Japan and England v New Zealand – are much stronger, and they are also better for Sunday, when Scotland play Argentina before South Africa and France contest the final.

Earlier this month, RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney admitted Twickenham was in “unchartered waters” with regard to the ticket sales for the inaugural tournament, which brings together all the major northern and southern hemisphere nations.

Speaking prior to its opening weekend earlier this month, Sweeney added: “This is the first time we’ve done this.

“A lot of fans are waiting to figure out who is playing who and when. You’ve got to go through those pool matches before you know you you’re playing on finals weekend. It’s a bit like a condensed World Cup.”

Nations Championship officials have been contacted for comment.

England will be selecting from a position of strength for Saturday’s immediate rematch against New Zealand after Fin Smith and Tommy Freeman were given the all-clear to train this week.

Smith suffered cramp during England’s record 37-12 victory over the All Blacks while Freeman was a late withdrawal from the right wing because of a thigh injury, resulting in Cadan Murley being thrust into the starting XV.

But both players have been included in a 37-man squad that will prepare for Saturday’s Allianz Stadium showdown that will decide who finishes third in the Nations Championship.

Noah Caluori has been added to the group as additional wing cover and in a major boost for head coach Steve Borthwick, no fresh injury concerns have arisen from the stunning five-try rout of New Zealand.

The result has been felt in the global rankings, with England climbing from fifth to fourth and the All Blacks plummeting from second to fifth.

Borthwick names his team on Wednesday with a sixth successive Test victory the target as England look to confirm their emergence as World Cup contenders next year.

title: England's haka response: World Rugby's regulations explained
article_text:
England could face another fine from World Rugby following their response to the All Blacks' haka at Allianz Stadium on Saturday.

Steve Borthwick's side produced a stunning 37-12 victory over New Zealand, but their actions before kick-off continue to generate debate.

Former England captain Lewis Moody joined the players on the pitch as part of his inspirational 'Front Up' campaign, which aims to raise funds and awareness for motor neurone disease.

England initially adopted a V-shaped formation before changing their positions during the haka.

However, Jamie George and Ollie Chessum appeared to cross the halfway line, potentially breaching World Rugby's protocol surrounding cultural challenges.

But what are teams actually allowed to do?

According to World Rugby's official Match Commissioner guidelines, there are clear restrictions surrounding cultural challenges.

These apply to both the team performing the haka and their opponents.

- The All Blacks must remain behind their own 10-metre line.

- England cannot advance beyond the halfway line.

- A minimum distance of 10 metres must separate the teams.

- England are under no obligation to face the haka.

- If both teams perform cultural challenges, a coin toss determines their positions.

Interestingly, there is nothing in the published protocol preventing England from forming a V shape. The potential breach concerns their position on the pitch.

England were famously fined £2,000 following their response to the haka before the 2019 Rugby World Cup semi-final.

Several England players crossed the halfway line in Yokohama, forcing referee Nigel Owens to intervene.

Ironically, then-All Blacks head coach Steve Hansen praised England's response, describing it as imaginative.

France were also fined £2,500 after advancing towards New Zealand before the 2011 Rugby World Cup final.

It is worth remembering that New Zealand are not exempt from these restrictions.

During their visit to Twickenham in November 2024, the All Blacks advanced beyond their own 10-metre line as England approached halfway.

That prompted questions over whether New Zealand Rugby could face punishment, although no subsequent fine was publicly reported.

However, the guidance does not specify a fixed financial penalty.

As of Tuesday morning, no fresh punishment has been publicly confirmed.

With England and the All Blacks set to meet again this Saturday, there will be plenty of interest in how Borthwick's players choose to respond this time.

title: NRLW breakout star Teagan Levi returns to sevens with golden ambition
article_text:
For many kids growing up playing sport in Australia, the ultimate dream is to wear green and gold on the world stage, to compete at an Olympic Games, or to play in one of the country’s premier domestic competitions.

Australia Sevens ace Teagan Levi has made all that a reality at just 23 years of age, and the multi-sport talent is now eyeing Olympic gold at the 2028 LA Games. “It just shows hard work really does beat talent,” Levi told RugbyPass after returning to sevens.

Levi has amassed one of the most diverse and remarkable sporting CVs in Australia, which began in Aussie Rules with the Gold Coast Suns. The Queenslander was taken sixth overall in the AFLW Draft but chose to pursue a rugby sevens career instead.

Five years later, Levi has played in front of 80,000 people at an Olympic Games and has tasted success multiple times on the HSBC SVNS Series. The 23-year-old isn’t one to back down from a challenge, and has been rewarded for that time and time again.

Levi hadn’t played rugby league before, but decided to spend the HSBC SVNS Series off-season with the Gold Coast Titans. The five-eighth was named the RLPA Rookie of the Year and earned a place in the Dally M Team of the Year, after the Titans reached the preliminary finals.

“It was a challenge but I did all the hard work before going there,” Levi said.

“It’s pretty similar to touch footy, which I played growing up. I knew those basic rules and I just knew if I backed myself and played the type of footy that I played, then the transition would be easy.

“I did all the hard work before I came across to make sure that I was being a better person and a better player.”

Levi added: “In sevens, yes it’s fast and quick but in league there’s no space. It looks like there’s space but actually the space closes up really fast. It was more creating the space for someone else rather than yourself.

“We just watched a video and it just showed how hard sevens actually is. The work rate, if you’re out on the field you don’t really get a rest.

“They’re both very different sports and they both have such a high standard that they play at.”

Levi captured national sporting headlines after a breakout season in the 13-player game, and is now looking to build on that experience back in rugby sevens. The playmaker spent about four weeks in pre-season before jetting off to Dubai for the HSBC SVNS Series opener.

World Rugby Breakthrough Player of the Year nominee Amelia Whitaker is the sole debutant in Australia’s 13-player group, with Isabella Nasser captaining the side. Levi is the second-most experienced squad member, just three events behind older sister Maddison.

“The girls have had an unreal pre-season. I’ve come back, this is week of pre-season so it’s’ been pretty tough,” Levi explained.

“I’m really excited to bae back and involved with these girls. They’re my sisters, they’re my family, we obviously travel the world together and we live out of each other’s pockets. But it’s really nice to come back into this group.

“They’re always welcoming with arms open and I think we’re building something really special. We don’t want to feel that feeling we did in Paris.

“The group that we have now is very exciting. There’s some younger girls that are coming through that will be a very good addition to our team. But then we also have the already experienced girls which will be amazing.”

The Levi sisters both starred as Australia claimed the circuit’s top prize in Bordeaux earlier this year, defeating arch-rivals New Zealand in a thrilling decider. Australia were crowned HSBC SVNS World Championship winners after claiming titles in Valladolid and southwestern France.

But a new season awaits, with an Olympic-qualifying year raising the stakes higher and adding another dimension to this sporting theatre. The Australians return to the UAE with fond memories of Dubai, having claimed silverware in five of the last six events.

Also, Australia only lost one to the New Zealanders across multiple pre-season matches, including a 2-0 sweep at the inaugural Kick On 7s. The women in gold are shaping us a leading SVNS contender once again – creating pressure the Aussies “walk towards.”

“Pressure is good but if we make sure that we go in prepared – the girls had a really good pre-season. They versed the Kiwis a few times, which is obviously our biggest rivalry… they only lost one game.

“Dubai sets a standard for the whole season to show teams that you’re here to play, you’re not just here to muck around.

“The lead-up to the ’28 Olympics starts now and we’ve definitely got the squad and the team to get that gold medal, and we’re striving to make sure that we never feel that feeling we did in Paris and the girls in Tokyo as well.”

title: Luke Jacobson to leave Chiefs for Bayonne after 2027, ending All Blacks eligibility
article_text:
Chiefs captain Luke Jacobson has signed a three-year deal with Bayonne, the Top 14 club announced on Monday 23 November. He will play a final season with the Chiefs in 2027 before joining the French side for 2028.

“Yeah, it’s a tough decision to leave NZR, Chiefs, Waikato, Hautapu, my home,” Jacobson said on social media, as RugbyPass reported his confirmed move to France. He added: “But I’ve still got one more year, and I’m focused on making the most of it.”

The Chiefs paid tribute to their captain in a statement on Monday. “As Chiefs captain, Jacobson has led by example, setting high standards and helping shape the culture of the team,” the club said.

The club added that Jacobson remains focused on his commitments to the team with another Super Rugby Pacific campaign ahead. It pointed to his recent trip to Japan, where he worked in a coaching role with the University of Waikato Chiefs Taua squad.

The Chiefs finished second in the 2026 Super Rugby season, losing heavily to the Hurricanes in the final, while also finishing second to them in the regular season.

The move will also affect his Test career. According to SA Rugby magazine, playing his club rugby in France will leave Jacobson ineligible for the All Blacks after the 2027 World Cup.

The magazine explained that selection requires an NZR contract and a place in New Zealand’s domestic system, though established All Blacks are occasionally allowed approved short-term spells overseas. Players returning to New Zealand from abroad must first play domestically before they can be selected again.

This has been seen most recently through the return of Richie Mo’unga, Reiko Ioane and Shannon Frizell, who all made returns to the black jersey after periods away. Frizell and Mo’unga had spent a spell in Japan, while Ioane spent a year in Dublin, where he won the URC with Leinster and reached the Champions Cup final.

Nicknamed “Concrete Shoulders” for his uncompromising tackling, Jacobson has played 30 Tests, the magazine said. His most recent came against Ireland in Auckland in July, during the Nations Championship and the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series. He also featured in three matches on New Zealand’s run to the 2023 World Cup final.

According to Planet Rugby’s report on his Chiefs exit, Jacobson made his debut in 2018, was named captain in 2024 and reached 100 matches this year.

Jacobson captained the All Blacks in 2026. RugbyPass said he first led them against the Sharks in Durban during Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry, having previously captained the Chiefs, Waikato and the New Zealand U20s, whom he led to the 2017 World Rugby Under 20 Championship title.

Luke Jacobson has played in 30 test matches for the All Blacks, with the most recent coming against the Springboks in the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry tour.

All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie has constantly praised Jacobson’s defensive work and leadership, the outlet added. He was ruled out of the Nations Championship’s November window, however, with an elbow injury that required surgery, RugbyPass reported.

Jacobson’s announcement came hours after reports that a Chiefs teammate is also heading to France, RugbyPass said. Wallace Sititi has reportedly signed with Top 14 club Stade Français, also for 2028.

title: Wallabies win over Wales far from perfect – but a lot better than recent weeks
article_text:
There have been times in the last six or seven weeks where Australian rugby fans have wondered when – or if – the next Wallabies win might come.

The Bledisloe Cup losses weren’t much fun, and there was a more than fair argument that the England and Scotland defeats, to start the November leg of the Nations Championship, were even worse. And knowing the Wallabies’ last two European tours both ended with a run of losses, it’s reasonable to assume that Australian confidence has taken a hit in recent times.

So it was pleasing to see the Wallabies start so well against Wales in Cardiff, adjust to the inevitable reactions, and complete the job at hand. Having spent the week celebrating maybe their greatest ever win, Wales were always going to be a tough prospect; the only unknowns were how much that masterful, but exhausting, win over New Zealand – and the aforementioned celebrations – had taken out of the Welsh players.

The look and feel of the Wallabies on attack had immediate hallmarks back to the first Nations Championship Tests in July, and even the win over South Africa in Perth in early September. Their 12-7 lead at half-time was the first time since that memorable win over the Springboks that Australia had led at the break.

Les Kiss and his players spoke last week again about wanting to dominate the collision area through physicality in their ball carrying, figuring that was a better way of securing faster ruck ball than addressing their lacklustre attacking clean-out.

Certainly, they did carry a lot better and it looked like there a was a plan to it. They changed the direction of their attack and forced the Welsh defenders into making decisions around whether to drift or to commit to a tackle.

With 465 metres gained, roughly a quarter of that beyond the point of contact, suggests they did a reasonable job of that. So does nine offloads to four, and 10 clean breaks to seven. Wales made many more entries into the Australian 22 than the Wallabies did into the Welsh red-zone – 20 to 9, in fact – but Australia were able to convert their opportunities into points with much greater efficiency.

As the game went on, the Wallabies’ confidence and ability to hold the ball for long periods increased. After Wales dominated possession for the best part of an hour, Australia finished with so much ball that the possession split for the game essentially evened out. Len Ikitau’s pick-and-drive try on the hour came after 24 phases, whereas against Scotland and England in the weeks prior, turnovers came in half that time.

Considering recent performances, it was just very satisfying on Sunday morning to be thinking and talking about all the things the Wallabies did well, rather than the other way around.

Did the improved physicality equate to faster ruck ball? Well, no, not really.

In the end, the Wallabies’ ball came back at an average of 2.67 seconds and nearly a whole second slower than what Wales enjoyed. The Welsh breakdown work was exceptional against New Zealand the week before and this just carried over to Saturday night in Cardiff.

That 2.67 second average ruck speed was basically the same as against Scotland the week before, which in turn was a shade slower than against England the week before that. Clearly, the Wallabies still have a bit of work to do there, if they really want to play with the speed of recycle they spoke repeatedly about in 2026.

But considering recent performances, it was just very satisfying on Sunday morning (Australian time) to be thinking and talking about all the things the Wallabies did well, rather than the other way around.

The win over Wales wasn’t perfect; far from it. But it was a lot better than what we’d seen in recent weeks and months, and that’s nothing to sneeze at, especially at this time of the rugby year, when many a Wallabies November northern campaign has come undone spectacularly. Indeed, November tours have cost past coaches their jobs, but that doesn’t feel like anything Kiss will need to worry about for now.

Ireland, in the fifth-sixth play-off at Twickenham on Friday, will present a different set of challenges. The Irish took the physicality and set-piece battle right to South Africa last Friday and came out on top. And Australia’s record against Ireland in recent years runs to four straight losses. Whether this one being on a neutral couple of acres of turf will help remains to be seen, but it’s a challenge the Wallabies will to be up for regardless.

There’s a small piece of history awaiting this current squad, and all it will take is their best performance of the year on a familiar plot of land in south-west London.

There’s further incentive for this playing group too. Not too many of them have enjoyed a winning season at international level, with the vast majority of them debuting after Michael Cheika’s 2019 squad enjoyed six wins from 10 games en route to a quarter-final exit at the Rugby World Cup that year.

There’s a small piece of history awaiting this current squad, and all it will take is their best performance of the year on a familiar plot of land in south-west London.

There are probably ways it could run smoother in future iterations, but on the whole, the Nations Championship has done exactly what was promised.

title: Six Nations relegation decision confirmed for 2030 as Georgia push for promotion
article_text:
The Six Nations countries could face relegation from rugby's new Nations Championship from 2030, but their places in the annual Six Nations tournament will remain untouched.

That is the key distinction as rugby's leading unions continue discussions over promotion and relegation.

England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales, France and Italy are all guaranteed their places in the Six Nations Championship, regardless of their results.

However, those same countries could eventually face relegation from the Nations Championship, the new global competition featuring the world's leading international sides.

And that could open the door for Georgia.

Under the existing agreement, promotion and relegation between the Nations Championship and the second-tier Nations Cup are scheduled to begin in 2030.

According to The Guardian, the Six Nations' official position remains that promotion and relegation should be introduced.

However, the precise system has yet to be finalised.

Some of rugby's leading unions are reportedly concerned about the financial consequences of dropping into the second tier.

Wales and Italy are among the countries mentioned in discussions about possible safeguards.

For example, Wales could theoretically finish bottom of the Nations Championship and lose their place in that competition under the proposed system.

They would still compete against England, Ireland, Scotland, France and Italy in the Six Nations every year.

The same would apply to any of the other five countries.

It means relegation could have serious financial and sporting consequences without changing the make-up of Europe's historic annual tournament.

Georgia have spent years campaigning for greater opportunities against rugby's established nations.

Their historic 13-12 victory over Wales in Cardiff in 2022 demonstrated their ability to compete against Six Nations opposition.

However, that result did not give them a pathway into the Six Nations Championship.

The Nations Cup could eventually offer something different.

Under the proposed promotion and relegation arrangements, Georgia could earn a place in the elite Nations Championship through their performances.

They would not, however, replace Wales or Italy in the Six Nations.

World Rugby has established a review group, chaired by chairman Brett Robinson, to examine how promotion and relegation could operate.

RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney has confirmed that the principle remains part of the plans, although several details still need to be resolved.

Financial protection for relegated unions is understood to be one of the biggest issues.

For Georgia, the opportunity is significant.

After years of knocking on the door, they could finally have a route into rugby's top international competition.

But for now, the Six Nations itself remains a closed shop.

title: All six Nations Championship final referees confirmed as controversial official appointed
article_text:
English referee Karl Dickson has been appointed to take charge of Sunday's Nations Championship final between France and South Africa.

It is an appointment that could bring plenty of scrutiny, given the controversy surrounding the Springboks and match officials during their last meeting with France.

Less than two weeks ago, France defeated South Africa in Paris, with Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus subsequently handed a six-match ban for his post-match comments about the officiating.

Jasper Wiese also received a red card during the match and was given a four-game suspension.

Erasmus was forced to watch the Springboks' next game from his hotel room, where he streamed a live watchalong, as he served the first part of his suspension.

With the two sides now preparing to meet again, this time with silverware on the line, Dickson could find himself under considerable pressure.

The Englishman has already found himself at the centre of controversy involving South Africa this year, following his performance in the fourth Test of the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry tour against New Zealand.

Rome, Italy - 23.02.2025: Referee Karl Dickson seen in action during the Guinness Six Nations 2025 match between Italy and France at Olympic Stadium. PUBLICATIONxNOTxINxITA Copyright: xMarcoxIacobucci/IPAxSportx/xipa-agency.netx/xx IPA_54494215 IPA_A

Dickson came under fire from the All Blacks camp after the Springboks' 43-28 victory in Baltimore, which secured a 3-1 series triumph for South Africa.

Several decisions attracted criticism, particularly an incident involving Cam Roigard, who was penalised for offside after being challenged without the ball.

New Zealand assistant coach Neil Barnes also questioned two early scrum penalties against Codie Taylor for failing to maintain his brake foot.

Barnes argued that both teams had committed similar offences and suggested South Africa were getting “the rub of the green” on tight decisions.

However, he was also quick to acknowledge that the Springboks deserved their victory.

Despite the criticism, Dickson remains widely regarded as one of the leading referees in world rugby.

A former professional scrum-half, he brings an understanding of the game that helps him manage the breakdown, maintain the flow of matches and communicate calmly under pressure.

His appointment to such a high-profile fixture is another show of faith in his ability to officiate at the highest level.

Dickson will be assisted by Andrew Brace and James Doleman for the France versus South Africa final, with Andrew Jackson appointed as television match official (TMO) and Richard Kelly as foul play review officer (FPRO).

Elsewhere, Angus Gardner will referee England's clash with New Zealand, while Pierre Brousset takes charge of Scotland against Argentina.

Luke Pearce will officiate Wales versus Japan, Nika Amashukeli has been appointed for Ireland against Australia, and Nic Berry will referee Italy against Fiji.
